pass_a_gloss: [...] having carried through the mystery of the economy with flesh. How then does he call [him] one about to [come], someone might perhaps say? For having set beside us the first man, and having made mention of the times of the transgression, he named the Christ as one going to be present after them, and last Adam; for he had been marked out beforehand, as in the willing and forethought of the God and Father, Saviour and Redeemer, but he shone forth at his own times, according to which the Ruler willed; and these are the ones in the last [times] and as it were at the settings of the present age. Therefore, having set the second into a type of the first, he all but inquires of the listener, saying the following as with a pause and a question: But is not, as the trespass, so also the free gift? For it is like as if he were saying: We have been condemned to the death through the transgression in Adam, the whole human nature having suffered this in him; for he was indeed firstfruit of the race; but in Christ we blossomed again into life; and Adam was a type of the one about to [come], that is of Christ, who brings in for us the grace equal in share to the left-handedness of those who came before. Have I then, he says, in saying this missed the true? Am I carried outside the fitting? Is not, as the trespass, so also the free gift? But was death strong through one, and will life be slack through one? And yet how is it not true to say that: For if by the trespass of the one the many died, much more the grace of God and the gift in grace of the one man Jesus Christ abounded into the many; for he will least of all endure, the creator being a lover of man, death to prevail through the one, and the life through one man to do nothing; and the grace will lie above the things from wrath. And not as through one having sinned [is] the gift. He refers, as it were, the nature of the matter and the force of the thought toward what is most fitting for God; for if indeed, he says, the condemnation from one, or through one, of Adam went off into all according to his likeness; for he was, as I said, the root of the race, having suffered the corruption; how would it not come to be both acceptable to faith and beloved to God that it is needful from one righteous act out of many trespasses for many to be justified? Or is the saving not to be chosen rather than the destroying, with God? Just as then Adam has been condemned, and the power of the curse prevailed over Moses, bearing under the corruption those on the earth, so, since Christ the second Adam has been justified, by the first road the justification will surely somewhere walk also into us. And we say Christ to have been justified, not as having become unrighteous at some time, yet having advanced from an increase toward the better things into justification, but because he himself first and alone man upon earth did not do sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. For if by the trespass of the one the death reigned through the one, and the rest. pass_b_english: …mystery of the dispensation in the flesh. How, then, does he call him “the one to come” (Romans 5:14)? someone might perhaps ask. For having set before us the first man and recalled the times of the transgression, he named Christ the one who would be present after those times, and the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45). He had indeed been foreordained as Saviour and Redeemer in the will and forethought of God the Father, but he appeared at his own proper times, those the Sovereign willed (1 Timothy 6:15); and these are the times at the end, at the sunset, as it were, of the present age.

So, having made the second correspond to the type of the first, he all but questions his hearer, speaking the next words with a pause, as a question: “But is it not so with the free gift as with the trespass?” (Romans 5:15). It is as if he were saying: We were condemned to death through the transgression in Adam, since the whole of human nature suffered this in him, for he was the firstfruits of the race; but in Christ we blossomed again into life. And Adam was a type of the one to come (Romans 5:14), that is, of Christ, who brings in for us a grace equal in measure to the perversity of those who went before. Have I, then, he says, missed the truth in saying this? Am I carried beyond what is reasonable? Is it not so with the free gift as with the trespass? Or did death prevail through one, while life through one will be powerless? And yet how is it not true to say this: “For if by the trespass of the one the many died, much more have the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abounded for the many” (Romans 5:15)? For the Creator, since he loves mankind, will by no means allow death to prevail through the one, and the life that comes through one man to accomplish nothing. Grace will rise above what comes from wrath.

“And the gift is not as it was through the one who sinned” (Romans 5:16). He refers, as it were, the nature of the matter and the force of the thought to what most befits God. For if, he says, the condemnation that came from one, that is, through one, Adam, passed on to all after his likeness (for, as I said, he was the root of the race and suffered corruption), how could it not be both acceptable to faith and dear to God that many should be justified from many trespasses by one act of righteousness (Romans 5:16)? Or is saving not what God prefers to destroying? Just as, then, Adam was condemned, and the power of the curse prevailed over Moses, making those on earth subject to corruption, so, since Christ, the second Adam, has been justified, justification will surely travel to us as well along the same road as the first. We say that Christ has been justified, not as though he had once been unrighteous and then advanced to justification by progress toward better things, but because he himself, first and alone of men on earth, “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22).

“For if, by the trespass of the one, death reigned through the one,” and so on (Romans 5:17). See again how he reckons the grace that justifies stronger than the curse that condemns. For no one, he says, could claim it was fitting that death through one should prevail over those on…

μετὰ σαρκὸς οἰκονομίας διαπεράναντος τὸ μυστήριον. πῶς οὖν μέλλοντα καλεῖ, φαίη
τις ἂν ἴσως; παραθεὶς γὰρ ἡμῖν τὸν πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον, καὶ τῶν τῆς παραβάσεως
διαμνημονεύσας καιρῶν, ὡς μετ' αὐτοὺς παρεσόμενόν τε καὶ ἔσχατον Ἀδὰμ ὠνόμασε
τὸν Χριστόν· προώριστο μὲν γὰρ ὡς ἐν θελήσει τε καὶ προμηθείᾳ τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρὸς
σωτήρ τε καὶ λυτρωτὴς, ἐπέφανε δὲ καιροῖς ἰδίοις καθ' οὓς ἠθέλησεν ὁ δυνάστης· οὗτοι
δέ εἰσιν οἱ ἐν ἐσχάτοις καὶ οἷον ἐπὶ δυσμαῖς τοῦ παρόντος αἰῶνος. οὐκοῦν τεθεικὼς εἰς
τύπον τοῦ πρώτου τὸν δεύτερον, μονονουχὶ καὶ διαπυνθάνεται τὸν ἀκροώμενον, ὡς ἐν
ὑποστιγμῇ τε καὶ ἐρωτήσει λέγων τὰ ἑξῆς· Ἀλλ' οὐχ ὡς τὸ παράπτωμα, οὕτω καὶ τὸ
χάρισμα; Ὅμοιον γὰρ ὡς λέγοι Κατακεκρίμεθα τῷ θανάτῳ διὰ τῆς ἐν Ἀδὰμ παραβάσεως,
ὅλης τῆς ἀνθρωπείας φύσεως τοῦτο παθούσης ἐν αὐτῷ· καὶ γὰρ ἦν ἀπαρχὴ τοῦ γένους·
ἀλλ' ἐν Χριστῷ πάλιν ἀνεθάλλομεν εἰς ζωήν· τύπος δὲ ἦν ὁ Ἀδὰμ τοῦ μέλλοντος,

τουτέστι Χριστοῦ, τῇ τῶν φθασάντων σκαιότητι τὴν ἰσομοιροῦσαν ἡμῖν εἰσκομίζοντος
χάριν· ἆρα οὖν, φησὶ, τοῦτο λέγων διημάρτηκα τἀληθοῦς; ἔξω φέρομαι τοῦ εἰκότος; οὐχ
ὡς τὸ παράπτωμα οὕτω καὶ τὸ χάρισμα; ἀλλ' ἴσχυσε μὲν δι' ἑνὸς ὁ θάνατος, ἀτονήσει δὲ
δι' ἑνὸς ἡ ζωή; καίτοι πῶς οὐκ ἀληθὲς ἐκεῖνο εἰπεῖν; εἰ γὰρ τῷ τοῦ ἑνὸς παραπτώματι οἱ
πολλοὶ ἀπέθανον, πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἡ χάρις τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ ἡ δωρεὰ ἐν χάριτι τῇ τοῦ ἑνὸς
ἀνθρώπου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ εἰς τοὺς πολλοὺς ὑπερίσσευσεν· ἀνέξεται γὰρ ἥκιστά γε,
φιλάνθρωπος ὢν ὁ δημιουργὸς, κατισχῦσαι μὲν θάνατον διὰ τοῦ ἑνὸς, ἀπρακτῆσαι δὲ
τὴν δι' ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ζωήν· ὑπερκείσεται δὲ ἡ χάρις τὰ ἐξ ὀργῆς.

review_notes: Old machine draft garbled the sense throughout: it made 'the last Adam' a name of Adam ('the one who would come ... is Adam, whom he has named the Christ'); turned the times of Christ's coming (οὗτοι = καιροί) into persons ('These are they who stand at the end'); read the second as a type of the first and 'tests the listener' for μονονουχὶ διαπυνθάνεται; rendered σκαιότητι as 'clumsiness' and attached it to the wrong clause; turned Cyril's rhetorical question 'did death prevail through one, while life through one will be powerless?' into an assertion that 'life is made ineffective'; put Cyril's own argument inside Paul's quotation marks; and omitted everything from 'the Creator, who loves mankind' onward (the Romans 5:16 lemma, the root-of-the-race argument, Adam/Moses and the second Adam, Christ 'justified' without prior unrighteousness with 1 Peter 2:22, and the Romans 5:17 lemma). Retranslated in full from the PG Greek. Scripture identified: Romans 5:14, 5:15 (Cyril reads it as a question), 5:16, 5:17; 1 Corinthians 15:45 (ἔσχατον Ἀδάμ); 1 Timothy 6:15 (καιροῖς ἰδίοις ... ὁ δυνάστης); 1 Peter 2:22 (wording exact; also Isaiah 53:9). κατεκράτησε δὲ Μωυσέως is rendered as written, 'prevailed over Moses' (genitive after κατακρατέω); a lost μέχρι ('until Moses', Romans 5:14) is possible, so check the printed PG page. Column number 185 and page number 4 dropped. Ends mid-sentence; u02-rem-mid continues γῆς.
